At p=0 every node links to its two nearest neighbors on each side; at p=0.2 three edges are rewired into accent-colored shortcuts across the ring; at p=1 most edges are rewired and the lattice is gone." width="100%"} Creates a ring lattice with rewiring probability `p`, producing graphs with high clustering and short path lengths. Small-world networks model many real-world phenomena. The construction has two steps. First, `n` new nodes are placed on a ring and each one is joined to its `k / 2` nearest neighbors on each side, giving `n * k / 2` edges. Then each of those edges is visited once and, with probability `p`, its far endpoint is replaced by a node chosen uniformly at random (never the node itself or one it is already joined to). Rewiring moves edges rather than adding them, so the edge count stays at `n * k / 2` for every `p`. In a directed graph each lattice edge points clockwise around the ring (from a node to the following ones) before rewiring. The `n` new nodes are unlabelled and get the next available node IDs. Existing nodes are left untouched and never connected to the new ones. Varying `p=` moves the graph between order and randomness: - `p=0.0` keeps the regular ring lattice: high clustering but long paths - small values such as `p=0.01` to `p=0.1` add a few long-range shortcuts that collapse path lengths while clustering stays high, the "small-world" regime - `p=1.0` rewires every edge, approaching a random graph with low clustering This makes the model a common choice for studying how local structure and shortcuts affect spreading processes, synchronization, and search in social, neural, and infrastructure networks. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes to add. Must be greater than `k=`, so the default `k=6` needs at least `7` nodes. [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[6]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of nearest neighbors each node is joined to in the starting ring lattice, split evenly between both sides (default `6`, i.e. three on each side). Must be even and less than `n=`. This sets the average degree of the result. `k=0` adds the nodes with no edges. [p]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[0.1]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Probability of rewiring each lattice edge, from `0.0` to `1.0` (default `0.1`). See the list above for how it shapes the result. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Integer seed for the random number generator. The same `seed=` with the same `n=`, `k=`, and `p=` always gives the same graph. If `None` (default), the result differs on every call (except with `p=0.0`, where no randomness is involved). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `k=` is odd or not less than `n=`, or if `p=` is outside `[0.0, 1.0]`. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~add_circulant_graph`) : Build a ring lattice, the graph before any rewiring. [](`~add_gnp_graph`) : Build a random graph with short paths but little clustering. [](`~transitivity`) : Measure the clustering that rewiring wears away. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In the Watts–Strogatz model the graph starts as a ring in which each node is joined to its `k` nearest neighbors, and then each edge is rewired with probability `p`. Rewiring never changes the edge count, which stays at `n * k / 2 = 300`: ::: {#c3c01ab9 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_smallworld_graph(n=100, k=6, p=0.1, seed=23) graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (100, 300) ``` ::: ::: A small rewiring probability shrinks the distances while barely denting the ring's high clustering, the hallmark of a small-world network. Comparing the average clustering coefficient and the diameter for `p=0.0`, `0.1` and `1.0` shows the diameter more than halving at `p=0.1` while the clustering stays high, whereas full rewiring destroys it: ::: {#d6773626 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} results = [] for p in (0.0, 0.1, 1.0): g = ec.Graph().add_smallworld_graph(n=100, k=6, p=p, seed=23) clustering = round(g.average_clustering_coefficient(), 3) results.append((p, clustering, g.diameter())) results ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [(0.0, 0.6, 17), (0.1, 0.473, 8), (1.0, 0.052, 5)] ``` ::: ::: ### A ring and a small world With `p=0.0` on the left there is no rewiring, so the result is the ring lattice: here each of `30` nodes is joined to the two nodes on either side, and the farthest nodes are `8` steps apart. With `p=0.1` on the right, a few edges become shortcuts across the ring, and the diameter falls to `5`: ::: {#bc0289ab .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ring = ec.Graph().add_smallworld_graph(n=30, k=4, p=0.0) small = ec.Graph().add_smallworld_graph(n=30, k=4, p=0.1, seed=23) ring.diameter(), small.diameter() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (8, 5) ``` ::: ::: ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#7ab813da .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} ring.layout_circular(order="id").plot( layout="pos", show_labels=False, node_size=5, width=320, height=320, legend=False, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
